beliefs: f shifts the first character forward by one within its Unicode category: lowercase a-z wrap, uppercase A-Z wrap, accented Latin letters shift to the next accented letter (é→ê, ñ→ò, ß→à), digits and other symbols unchanged [E1, E3, E7]
f leaves the middle characters (positions 1..n-1) unchanged [E1, E2, E3, E4]
f appends a literal 'y' to the end of the string, but only if the string does not already end in 'y' [E5]
Single-character input 'y' returns 'z' (shifted, no append since it already ends in y) [E4, E5]
When the first character is a digit, it is NOT shifted: '0a'->'0ay', '9z'->'9zy', '123'->'123y' [E1, E3]
The trailing 'y' is appended for non-empty inputs not ending in 'y', including digit-first ones ('0a'->'0ay', '9'->'9y') [E1, E2, E3]
The append is suppressed when the input already ends in 'y': 'ay'->'by', 'yyy'->'zyy', 'Yy'->'Zy' [E5]
Accented/non-ASCII letters are shifted to the next letter in their Unicode block (é→ê, É→Ê, ñ→ò, ß→à), not left unchanged [E7]
How exactly to shift arbitrary Unicode letters (e.g. ß→à, ñ→ò) is unclear; I approximate by incrementing the codepoint for Latin-1 accented letters? [E7]
notes: E7 shows accented letters are shifted like letters, not left unchanged. I extended the shift to Latin-1 accented letters by codepoint increment (é→ê, É→Ê, ñ→ò, ß→à), which matches all E7 outputs; the exact rule for arbitrary Unicode letters remains a guess.
